text: Single values only get you so far. Lists and dictionaries are how Python holds more than one value at a time — and they show up constantly in this course.

A list holds values in order, accessed by position. Zero gets you the first element, negative one gets you the last. And lists are mutable — append adds a new one right onto the end, no rebuilding required.

A dictionary holds values by name instead of position — a key, and a value. This should look familiar. It's structurally identical to Lesson 8's JSON object, and that's not a coincidence — Lesson 24 reads real JSON and hands you back exactly this.

Put a bunch of dictionaries into a list, and you get something that looks a lot like rows in a table — because that's exactly what it is. This is the precise shape you get back from reading a JSON file full of records, and it's what a Pandas DataFrame, coming up in Lesson 21, formalizes into something far more powerful.
Position for lists, name for dictionaries, and a list of dictionaries is basically a table already. Next lesson: conditions — making decisions based on a value. See you there.
